To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) radiation triggers oxidative stress that can damage DNA and proteins involved in DNA replication/repair; (ii) the resulting protein damage can compromise DNA repair/replica- tion, leading to cell death; and (iii) the effects of protein damage can be mitigated by strong antioxidant defenses.

(1) oxidative stress is an unavoidable by-product of exposure to ionizing radiation and (2) oxidative stress can have a variety or subtle and profound effects, including interactions with DNA damage, which can be modeled using mathematical equations.

(i) the model of oxidative stress-induced protein damage is consistent with experimental data on survival of the extremely radiation-resistant bacterium Deinococcus radio durans after high doses of acute and chronic ionizing irradiation; (ii) the model can potentially be generalized for use in other organisms and at lower radiation doses; and (iii) our results suggest that the model may be useful in the development of new strategies to protect normal tissues against the effects of radiation therapy and to protect astronauts against the effects
In summary, our research is concerned with
modeling of interactions between radiation and oxidative stress, and the resulting damage to DNA and proteins.
the hypothesis that radiation-induced oxidative stress can have profound effects on the ability of an organism to repair radiation damage to DNA.
the hypothesis that radiation-induced oxidative stress and DNA damage interact synergistically to affect the biological response to radiation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
oxidative damage to DNA repair proteins is an important factor in the survival of D. radiodurans at high doses of ionizing radiation.
the radiation-induced oxidative stress is not only a cause of damage to DNA, but also a cause of damage in proteins involved in DNA replication and repair.
radiation-induced oxidative stress can have both positive and negative effects on the repair of DSBs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the radiation dose and the rate of oxidative stress production are the key factors in determining whether radiation damage to DNA will be exacerbated or alleviated by radiation damage to proteins involved with repair/replication.
oxidative stress is a significant factor in the response of D. radiodurans to high doses of radiation.

radiation-induced oxidative stress can be a double-edged sword: it is essential for the killing effect of high doses of radiation, but can be beneficial for the repair of radiation damage to DNA at low doses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
radiation damage is a complex phenomenon involving interactions between DNA damage and damage to proteins involved with DNA repair/replications.
radiation-induced oxidative stress can be a significant factor in the biological response to ionizing radiation.
the effects of ionizing radiation on DNA damage and repair may be more complicated than is generally assumed.
